newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Journalists urges freedom in post-handover HK.
newsitem.headline: Journalists urges freedom in post-handover HK.

text.p: The Commonwealth Journalists Association (CJA) urged China on Friday to respect the press and freedom of expression in Hong Kong after it takes back the territory on July 1.

"The CJA believes there is a moral and legal obligation under the Sino-British Joint Declaration to ensure that human rights, including freedom of expression and of the press, are upheld and safeguarded after the handover," the CJA said.
It made the comments in a statement released at the end of a five-day conference it organised in Hong Kong.

The Joint Declaration is the 1984 treaty governing Hong Kong's handover, which promises the territory a high degree of autonomy, including the maintenance of its freedoms and capitalist way of life for 50 years.
The CJA said Britain and other Commonwealth countries must closely monitor human rights in Hong Kong after the handover.
The 53-member Commonwealth mainly groups Britain and its former colonies.

"In the event of human rights obligations being breached, the CJA strongly urges the British government to pursue all possible avenues of redress, including recourse to the international courts," it said.

Press freedom is one of the burning issues as the British colony's 6.3 million people prepare to revert to Beijing rule. A China-controlled panel has listed 25 Hong Kong laws for repeal or amendment after the handover, including parts of the Bill of Rights and two laws that allow political demonstrations and the free association of groups such as political parties.
The plan has sparked outrage from Hong Kong's pro-democracy parties and earned China forceful objections from Britain and the United States.
China also plans to scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature.
The conference attracted 73 journalists from 26 countries and was the last major Commonwealth event held in Hong Kong before the handover, the CJA said.
